claim: Bestrophin (BEST1-4) ligand-gated chloride (Cl-) channels are activated by calcium (Ca2+).
source: Bestrophin (BEST1-4) ligand-gated chloride (Cl-) channels are activated by calcium (Ca2+).
evidence: This is a well-established property of bestrophin channels stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutation of BEST1 causes retinal disease.
source: Mutation of BEST1 causes retinal disease.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Bestrophin channels have no sequence or structural similarity to other ion channels.
source: Partly because bestrophin channels have no sequence or structural similarity to other ion channels, the molecular mechanisms underlying gating are unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparisons in the introduction.

claim: Opening of the bestrophin pore is due to the repositioning of tethered pore-lining helices within a surrounding protein shell.
source: Unlike other channels, opening of the pore is due to the repositioning of tethered pore-lining helices within a surrounding protein shell that dramatically widens a neck of the pore through a concertina of amino acid rearrangements.
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM structures showing conformational changes between open and closed states.

claim: The neck serves as both the activation and the inactivation gate in bestrophin channels.
source: The neck serves as both the activation and the inactivation gate.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing the neck in different conformational states and by previous electrophysiological studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+ binding instigates opening of the neck through allosteric means.
source: Ca2+ binding instigates opening of the neck through allosteric means whereas inactivation peptide binding induces closing.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons of Ca2+-bound and Ca2+-free states and by the W287F mutation studies.

claim: Inactivation peptide binding induces closing of the neck.
source: Ca2+ binding instigates opening of the neck through allosteric means whereas inactivation peptide binding induces closing.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing the inactivation peptide bound in closed conformations and by previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: An aperture within the pore controls anion permeability.
source: An aperture within the otherwise wide pore controls anion permeability.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis studies of V205 and permeability measurements with different anions.

claim: The family of bestrophin proteins (BEST1-4) was identified by linkage analysis to hereditary macular degenerations caused by mutations in BEST1.
source: The family of bestrophin proteins (BEST1-4) was identified by linkage analysis to hereditary macular degenerations caused by mutations in BEST1 (Petrukhin et al., 1998; Marquardt et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: More than 200 mutations in BEST1 are linked with eye disease.
source: To date more than 200 mutations in BEST1 are linked with eye disease (Johnson et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: BEST1-4 proteins are expressed in the plasma membrane and form Ca2+-activated Cl- channels by assembling as pentamers.
source: BEST1-4 proteins are expressed in the plasma membrane and form Ca2+-activated Cl- channels by assembling as pentamers (Hartzell et al., 2008; Kane Dickson et al., 2014; Vaisey et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2002; Tsunenari et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and by the structural data showing pentameric assembly.

claim: BEST1 mediates a Ca2+-activated Cl- current that is integral to human retinal pigment epithelial function.
source: Data indicate that BEST1 mediates a Ca2+-activated Cl- current that is integral to human retinal pigment epithelial function (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Chicken BEST1 shares 74% sequence identity with human BEST1.
source: An X-ray structure of chicken BEST1, which shares 74% sequence identity with human BEST1 and possesses analogous Ca2+-activation and anion-selectivity properties, revealed an architecture that is distinct from other ion channel families (Kane Dickson et al., 2014; Vaisey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison and the cited references.

claim: Chicken BEST1 possesses analogous Ca2+-activation and anion-selectivity properties to human BEST1.
source: An X-ray structure of chicken BEST1, which shares 74% sequence identity with human BEST1 and possesses analogous Ca2+-activation and anion-selectivity properties, revealed an architecture that is distinct from other ion channel families (Kane Dickson et al., 2014; Vaisey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The bestrophin channel comprises five BEST1 subunits arranged symmetrically around a central ion pore that is ~95 Å long.
source: The channel comprises five BEST1 subunits arranged symmetrically around a central ion pore that is ~95 Å long.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data from X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM.

claim: The diameter of the bestrophin pore varies along its length and contains two constrictions, the 'neck' and the 'aperture', both of which are lined by hydrophobic amino acids.
source: The diameter of the pore varies along its length and contains two constrictions, the 'neck' and the 'aperture', both of which are lined by hydrophobic amino acids.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and pore dimension analysis.

claim: KpBest shares minimal (14%) sequence identity with human BEST1.
source: The X-ray structure of a bestrophin channel from the prokaryotic organism Klebsiella pneumoniae (KpBest) revealed a similar architecture, including analogous neck and aperture regions, in spite of minimal (14%) sequence identity to human BEST1 (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison and the cited reference.

claim: Metazoan bestrophin channels are anion-selective and activated by Ca2+.
source: Surprisingly, however, whereas metazoan bestrophin channels are anion-selective and activated by Ca2+, KpBest is cation-selective and does not contain the Ca2+ sensor region (the 'Ca2+ clasp') that is conserved amongst metazoan organisms.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data and structural comparisons.

claim: KpBest is cation-selective and does not contain the Ca2+ sensor region (the 'Ca2+ clasp') that is conserved amongst metazoan organisms.
source: Surprisingly, however, whereas metazoan bestrophin channels are anion-selective and activated by Ca2+, KpBest is cation-selective and does not contain the Ca2+ sensor region (the 'Ca2+ clasp') that is conserved amongst metazoan organisms.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and the cited reference.

claim: Ca2+-activation of chicken BEST1 is due to the binding of Ca2+ ions to the cytosolic Ca2+ clasps and to subsequent conformational changes in the neck.
source: From electrophysiological studies of purified chicken BEST1 and of mutants inspired by the structure, it was deduced that Ca2+-activation of the channel is due to the binding of Ca2+ ions to the cytosolic Ca2+ clasps, of which there are five owing to the pentameric architecture, and to subsequent conformational changes in the neck (Vaisey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and by the structural data presented in this manuscript.

claim: The neck forms the activation gate that opens in response to the binding of cytosolic Ca2+ ions.
source: These experiments made it clear that the neck forms the activation gate that opens in response to the binding of cytosolic Ca2+ ions.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological studies and structural data.

claim: Mutation of F80 and F84 to alanine had no effect on the ion selectivity properties of the channel.
source: However, we found that mutation of these residues to alanine had no effect on the ion selectivity properties of the channel, which made it seem unlikely that permeation through the neck was facilitated by anion-quadropole interactions in the wild type channel (Vaisey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Molecular simulation studies suggested that the conformation of the neck observed in the X-ray structure would form a significant energetic barrier that would likely prevent ion permeation.
source: Further, molecular simulation studies suggested that the conformation of the neck observed in the X-ray structure would form a significant energetic barrier that would likely prevent ion permeation (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: BEST1 undergoes inactivation wherein ionic currents through BEST1 decrease over time.
source: Our recent electrophysiological studies using purified chicken BEST1 in synthetic bilayers show that, like many ion channels, BEST1 undergoes inactivation wherein ionic currents through BEST1 decrease over time (Vaisey and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Channel inactivation is an inherent property of bestrophin channels and not due to other cellular factors.
source: We now realize that the 'current rundown' previously observed for mammalian bestrophin channels is due to channel inactivation and that channel inactivation is an inherent property of bestrophin channels and not due to other cellular factors.
evidence: This is supported by studies using purified channels in synthetic bilayers.

claim: Inactivation is stimulated by high (>500 nM) concentrations of Ca2+.
source: Inactivation is stimulated by high (>500 nM) concentrations of Ca2+ and is caused by the binding of a C-terminal 'inactivation peptide', contained within amino acids 346–367, to a receptor on the channel's cytosolic surface that is located near the Ca2+ clasp (Vaisey and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Inactivation is caused by the binding of a C-terminal 'inactivation peptide', contained within amino acids 346–367, to a receptor on the channel's cytosolic surface that is located near the Ca2+ clasp.
source: Inactivation is stimulated by high (>500 nM) concentrations of Ca2+ and is caused by the binding of a C-terminal 'inactivation peptide', contained within amino acids 346–367, to a receptor on the channel's cytosolic surface that is located near the Ca2+ clasp (Vaisey and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and by structural data showing the inactivation peptide bound.

claim: Inactivation can be substantially diminished by mutation of the receptor site or mutation of the inactivation peptide.
source: Inactivation can be substantially diminished by mutation of the receptor site or mutation of the inactivation peptide, and it can be prevented altogether by removal of the inactivation peptide (Vaisey and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Inactivation can be prevented altogether by removal of the inactivation peptide.
source: Inactivation can be substantially diminished by mutation of the receptor site or mutation of the inactivation peptide, and it can be prevented altogether by removal of the inactivation peptide (Vaisey and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and by the BEST1345 construct used in this study.

claim: The neck functions as the inactivation gate that prevents ion flow in the inactivated state.
source: From these and other mutagenesis studies it was additionally concluded that the neck functions as the inactivation gate that prevents ion flow in the inactivated state (Vaisey and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and by structural data.

claim: The antibody 10D10 stimulates inactivation of BEST1.
source: Electrophysiological analyses of the antibody's effect on BEST1 currents recorded using purified channels that were reconstituted into lipid bilayers indicate that it stimulates inactivation (Vaisey and Long, 2018), providing further evidence that the X-ray structure represents an inactivated state of the channel.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The X-ray structure of BEST1 represents an inactivated state in which the neck is too narrow to allow ions to flow through it.
source: Thus, because the inactivation peptide is bound to its receptor in the X-ray structure and because the antibody used for co-crystallization stimulates inactivation, we suspect that the X-ray structure represents an inactivated state in which the neck is too narrow to allow ions to flow through it (Kane Dickson et al., 2014; Vaisey and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and the cited references.

claim: A 3.1 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of Ca2+-bound BEST1405 without an antibody is indistinguishable from the previously published X-ray structure.
source: The conformation of the channel is indistinguishable from the previously published X-ray structure (Kane Dickson et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplements 1,2, RMSD for Cα atoms = 0.5 Å).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison showing RMSD of 0.5 Å.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of Ca2+-bound BEST1405 represents a Ca2+-bound inactivated state.
source: As in the X-ray structure, each of the inactivation peptides, of which there are five owing to the symmetry of the channel, is bound to its cytosolic receptor and well defined in the density. Therefore, this cryo-EM structure also represents a Ca2+-bound inactivated state.
evidence: This is supported by the presence of bound inactivation peptides in the structure.

claim: BEST1345 does not inactivate because it is missing the C-terminal inactivation peptide.
source: BEST1345 does not inactivate because it is missing the C-terminal inactivation peptide (Vaisey and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: BEST1345 possesses normal Cl- selectivity and Ca2+-dependent activation.
source: Importantly, whilst it does not inactivate, we have previously shown that BEST1345 possesses normal Cl- selectivity and Ca2+-dependent activation (Vaisey and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Single particle cryo-EM analysis of Ca2+-bound BEST1345 revealed two distinct conformations of the channel.
source: Single particle cryo-EM analysis of Ca2+-bound BEST1345 (Figure 1—figure supplements 2,3) revealed two distinct conformations of the channel (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by 3D classification of the cryo-EM data.

claim: The first conformation of Ca2+-bound BEST1345, determined at 3.0 Å resolution, represents 86% of the particles and is essentially indistinguishable from the structure of BEST1405, except for the absence of the inactivation peptide.
source: The first, determined at 3.0 Å resolution, represents 86% of the particles and is essentially indistinguishable from the structure of BEST1405, except for the absence of the inactivation peptide (Figure 1A,C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, RMSD for Cα atoms = 0.5 Å).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison showing RMSD of 0.5 Å.

claim: The first conformation of Ca2+-bound BEST1345 represents a Ca2+-bound closed conformation.
source: Because BEST1345 does not inactivate, the structure presumably represents a Ca2+-bound closed conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that BEST1345 does not inactivate and the neck is closed.

claim: The conformation in which the activation gate (the neck) is closed even though Ca2+ is bound is consistent with single channel recordings of drosophila BEST1, which indicate that the channel has a low probability of being open.
source: The conformation, in which the activation gate (the neck) is closed even though Ca2+ is bound, is consistent with single channel recordings of drosophila BEST1, which indicate that the channel has a low probability of being open (Chien et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The second conformation of Ca2+-bound BEST1345, which represents 14% of the particles and is determined to 2.9 Å resolution, contains a dramatically widened pore within the neck.
source: The second conformation present within the cryo-EM dataset, which represents 14% of the particles and is determined to 2.9 Å resolution, contains a dramatically widened pore within the neck (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and pore dimension analysis.

claim: The second conformation of Ca2+-bound BEST1345 represents the open conformation of the channel.
source: Based on discussions presented herein we conclude that this represents the open conformation of the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the widened neck and the ability to allow ion permeation.

claim: The relative abundance of the closed conformation suggests that it is energetically favorable.
source: The relative abundance of the closed conformation suggests that it is energetically favorable.
evidence: This is inferred from the 86% vs 14% distribution of particles.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of BEST1345 in the absence of Ca2+ is determined to 3.0 Å resolution.
source: To address how Ca2+ binding contributes to BEST1 channel gating, we determined the cryo-EM structure of BEST1345 in the absence of Ca2+ (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2). The structure is determined to 3.0 Å resolution and is indistinguishable from a cryo-EM structure of Ca2+-free BEST1405 at 3.6 Å resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The inactivation peptide is not bound to its receptor in the structure of BEST1405 without Ca2+.
source: As was expected from biochemical and electrophysiological analyses (Vaisey and Long, 2018), the inactivation peptide is not bound to its receptor in the structure of BEST1405 without Ca2+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and the cited reference.

claim: The neck is closed in the absence of Ca2+.
source: The neck is closed in the absence of Ca2+ (Figure 3A), and notably, it shares the same closed conformation as in the inactivated and Ca2+-bound closed structures (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: Without Ca2+, the majority of each Ca2+ clasp becomes disordered.
source: Without Ca2+, the majority of each Ca2+ clasp becomes disordered (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by missing density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: 3D classification of the Ca2+-free BEST1345 dataset indicated a degree of flexibility in the channel between the transmembrane and cytosolic regions that was manifested as a ~ 5° rotation along the symmetry axis.
source: 3D classification of the Ca2+-free BEST1345 dataset yielded only closed conformations of the neck but did indicate a degree of flexibility in the channel between the transmembrane and cytosolic regions that was manifested as a ~ 5° rotation along the symmetry axis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by 3D classification analysis.

claim: The conformational flexibility observed in Ca2+-free BEST1345 was not observed in the Ca2+-bound datasets, which suggests that Ca2+ binding rigidifies the channel.
source: This conformational flexibility was not observed in the Ca2+-bound datasets, which suggests that Ca2+ binding rigidifies the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of 3D classification results.

claim: Ca2+-dependent rigidification may be necessary for opening of the neck.
source: We hypothesize that this Ca2+-dependent rigidification may be necessary for opening of the neck.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observations.

claim: In the closed conformation, the neck is less than 3.5 Å in diameter and approximately 15 Å long.
source: In the closed conformation, the neck is less than 3.5 Å in diameter and approximately 15 Å long; three hydrophobic amino acids on the neck helix (S2b) from each of the channel's five subunits, I76, F80 and F84, form its walls (Figure 1C,E,F) (Kane Dickson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by pore dimension analysis from the structures.

claim: Three hydrophobic amino acids on the neck helix (S2b) from each of the channel's five subunits, I76, F80 and F84, form the walls of the neck.
source: In the closed conformation, the neck is less than 3.5 Å in diameter and approximately 15 Å long; three hydrophobic amino acids on the neck helix (S2b) from each of the channel's five subunits, I76, F80 and F84, form its walls (Figure 1C,E,F) (Kane Dickson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: The narrowness, length and hydrophobicity of the closed neck would create an energetic barrier to ion permeation.
source: Its narrowness, length and hydrophobicity would create an energetic barrier to ion permeation, consistent with simulation studies of wild-type and neck mutant BEST1 channel structures (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited simulation studies.

claim: In the open conformation, the neck has dilated to approximately 13 Å in diameter.
source: In the open conformation, the neck has dilated to approximately 13 Å in diameter, which is more than sufficient to allow permeation of hydrated Cl- ions (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by pore dimension analysis from the structures.

claim: The diameter of the open neck is more than sufficient to allow permeation of hydrated Cl- ions.
source: In the open conformation, the neck has dilated to approximately 13 Å in diameter, which is more than sufficient to allow permeation of hydrated Cl- ions (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the diameter measurement and the size of hydrated Cl- ions.

claim: No appreciable conformational difference is present in the cytosolic region of the channel between open and closed conformations.
source: No appreciable conformational difference is present in the cytosolic region of the channel, and in particular, the aperture constriction of the pore retains its dimensions.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The aperture constriction of the pore retains its dimensions between open and closed conformations.
source: No appreciable conformational difference is present in the cytosolic region of the channel, and in particular, the aperture constriction of the pore retains its dimensions.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The neck functions as a gate that permits ion flow in the open conformation and prevents it in the closed conformation.
source: In accord with conclusions drawn from previous electrophysiological studies of mutations made within the neck and aperture (Vaisey et al., 2016; Vaisey and Long, 2018), we conclude that the neck functions as a gate. It permits ion flow in the open conformation and prevents it in the closed conformation.
evidence: This is supported by structural data and cited electrophysiological studies.

claim: Opening of the neck is reminiscent of the dilation of the iris of a camera lens.
source: Figure 2 and Figure 2—video 1 depict the transition between the closed and open conformations of the neck. Opening is reminiscent of the dilation of the iris of a camera lens.
evidence: This is a descriptive analogy based on the structural changes observed.

claim: Conformational changes in the helices that form the walls of the neck (the S2b 'neck' helices from each of the five subunits) underlie opening.
source: Conformational changes in the helices that form the walls of the neck (the S2b 'neck' helices from each of the five subunits) underlie opening.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison of open and closed states.

claim: Each S2b 'neck' helix is flanked on both of its ends by loop-like regions of extended secondary structure that partition what would otherwise be a continuous α-helix into three segments – S2a, S2b and S2c.
source: Unlike most ion channels in which transmembrane segments are entirely α-helical, each S2b 'neck' helix is flanked on both of its ends by loop-like regions of extended secondary structure that partition what would otherwise be a continuous α-helix into three segments – S2a, S2b and S2c (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: The loop-like regions flanking the S2b helix provide a degree of flexibility that allows the neck helices to adopt their open and closed conformations.
source: From comparison of the open and closed conformations of the neck, it is apparent that these loop-like regions provide a degree of flexibility that allows the neck helices to adopt their open and closed conformations and also provide a degree of tethering to the ends of these helices.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison.

claim: The loop-like regions flanking the S2b helix provide a degree of tethering to the ends of these helices.
source: From comparison of the open and closed conformations of the neck, it is apparent that these loop-like regions provide a degree of flexibility that allows the neck helices to adopt their open and closed conformations and also provide a degree of tethering to the ends of these helices.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison.

claim: While the neck helices undergo substantial movement, the S2a and S2c helices remain essentially fixed during the gating transition.
source: Consequently, while the neck helices undergo substantial movement, the S2a and S2c helices remain essentially fixed during the gating transition.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: In the closed conformation of the neck, hydrophobic packing at the center of the neck among the I76, F80 and F84 residues themselves stabilize this conformation.
source: In the closed conformation of the neck, hydrophobic packing at the center of the neck among the I76, F80 and F84 residues themselves stabilize this conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement of these residues.

claim: In the open conformation, the tendency of the phenylalanine residues to seclude their hydrophobicity from an aqueous environment is satisfied by their interactions with other hydrophobic amino acids (Y236 and W287) on the S3b and S4a helices located behind the neck helix.
source: In the open conformation, the tendency of the phenylalanine residues to seclude their hydrophobicity from an aqueous environment is satisfied by their interactions with other hydrophobic amino acids (Y236 and W287) on the S3b and S4a helices located behind the neck helix (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement in the open state.

claim: The conformational change moves F80 and F84 away from the center of the pore and involves rotation of the neck helix along its helical axis (~15 ° clockwise viewed from the extracellular side).
source: The conformational change moves F80 and F84 away from the center of the pore and involves rotation of the neck helix along its helical axis (~15 ° clockwise viewed from the extracellular side) and outward displacement of the neck helix that is more pronounced on its N-terminal end (~2.5 Å at F80).
evidence: This is measured from structural comparison.

claim: The conformational change involves outward displacement of the neck helix that is more pronounced on its N-terminal end (~2.5 Å at F80).
source: The conformational change moves F80 and F84 away from the center of the pore and involves rotation of the neck helix along its helical axis (~15 ° clockwise viewed from the extracellular side) and outward displacement of the neck helix that is more pronounced on its N-terminal end (~2.5 Å at F80).
evidence: This is measured from structural comparison.

claim: The opening transition includes a slight expansion of the entire transmembrane region of the channel (~1 Å increase in radius).
source: The opening transition includes a slight expansion of the entire transmembrane region of the channel (~1 Å increase in radius), and a coordinated set of side chain rotamer changes (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is measured from structural comparison.

claim: Both F80 and F84 move from the most commonly observed rotamer for phenylalanine in the closed conformation to the second most commonly-observed rotamer in the open conformation.
source: Both F80 and F84 move from the most commonly observed rotamer for phenylalanine (observed 44% of the time in the PDB) in the closed conformation to the second most commonly-observed rotamer (observed 33% of the time) in the open conformation (Lovell et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by rotamer analysis and the cited reference.

claim: F80 and F84 rotate away from the axis of the pore by 80° and 105°, respectively.
source: By these conformational changes, F80 and F84 rotate away from the axis of the pore (by 80o and 105o, respectively, Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured from structural comparison.

claim: Accompanying side chain rotamer changes occur among neighboring residues (Y236, F282, F283, and W287) to allow for the movements of F80 and F84.
source: Accompanying side chain rotamer changes that occur among neighboring residues (Y236, F282, F283, and W287) allow for the movements of F80 and F84 (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: When the channel opens, the first α-helical turn of the neck helix unravels such that I76 packs with F247, F276, L279 and F283 in the open conformation and has shifted by approximately 10 Å.
source: When the channel opens, the first α-helical turn of the neck helix unravels such that I76 packs with F247, F276, L279 and F283 in the open conformation and has shifted by approximately 10 Å (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured from structural comparison.

claim: The unraveling of the first α-helical turn of the neck helix is facilitated by P77, which is perfectly conserved among BEST channels.
source: The unraveling is facilitated by P77, which is perfectly conserved among BEST channels and is part of the neck helix in its closed conformation, but marks its N-terminal end in the open conformation (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and sequence conservation.

claim: P77 is part of the neck helix in its closed conformation, but marks its N-terminal end in the open conformation.
source: The unraveling is facilitated by P77, which is perfectly conserved among BEST channels and is part of the neck helix in its closed conformation, but marks its N-terminal end in the open conformation (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: The repositioning within the neck exposes the hydrophilic residues S79 and G83 on the neck helix to the pore in its open conformation.
source: The repositioning within the neck also exposes the hydrophilic residues S79 and G83 on the neck helix, which had been secluded behind the F80 and F84, to the pore in its open conformation (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: S79 and G83 had been secluded behind F80 and F84 in the closed conformation.
source: The repositioning within the neck also exposes the hydrophilic residues S79 and G83 on the neck helix, which had been secluded behind the F80 and F84, to the pore in its open conformation (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: Through a concertina of coordinated conformational changes in and around the neck helix, amino acids that formed the hydrophobic barrier that prevented ion permeation have dispersed and reveal a wide aqueous vestibule.
source: Thus, through a concertina of coordinated conformational changes in and around the neck helix, amino acids that formed the hydrophobic barrier that prevented ion permeation have dispersed and reveal a wide aqueous vestibule, the diameter of which would be large enough to allow permeation of hydrated halide ions and larger molecules as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural changes observed.

claim: The diameter of the open neck would be large enough to allow permeation of hydrated halide ions and larger molecules as well.
source: Thus, through a concertina of coordinated conformational changes in and around the neck helix, amino acids that formed the hydrophobic barrier that prevented ion permeation have dispersed and reveal a wide aqueous vestibule, the diameter of which would be large enough to allow permeation of hydrated halide ions and larger molecules as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured diameter of the open neck.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of BEST1345 in the absence of Ca2+ is indistinguishable from a cryo-EM structure of Ca2+-free BEST1405 at 3.6 Å resolution.
source: The structure is determined to 3.0 Å resolution and is indistinguishable from a cryo-EM structure of Ca2+-free BEST1405 at 3.6 Å resolution.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The overall structure of the Ca2+-free channel is very similar to the inactivated and Ca2+-bound closed conformations with the only notable differences near the Ca2+ clasp.
source: The overall structure of the channel is very similar to the inactivated and Ca2+-bound closed conformations with the only notable differences near the Ca2+ clasp.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: W287 is perfectly conserved among metazoan bestrophin channels and even conserved in the prokaryotic KpBEST channel.
source: W287 is perfectly conserved among metazoan bestrophin channels and even conserved in the prokaryotic KpBEST channel (Yang et al., 2014) (Figure 4A); this sequence conservation would be consistent with an important role in channel gating.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and the cited reference.

claim: W287 is positioned approximately at the midpoint between the Ca2+ clasp and the neck.
source: W287 is also positioned approximately at the midpoint between the Ca2+ clasp and the neck (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is observed from the structure.

claim: W287 adopts one side chain rotamer to pack with F80 and F84 in the open conformation and a different side chain rotamer in the closed conformation that buttresses the space between adjacent neck helices.
source: W287 adopts one side chain rotamer to pack with F80 and F84 in the open conformation and a different side chain rotamer in the closed conformation that buttresses the space between adjacent neck helices (Figure 2A,B, Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: The W287F mutation produces channels with dramatically altered gating.
source: We find that the W287F mutation (BEST1345 W287F) produces channels with dramatically altered gating.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: BEST1345 W287F retained normal Cl- versus K+ selectivity.
source: Whilst BEST1345 W287F retained normal Cl- versus K+ selectivity (Figure 4B), the W287F mutation constitutively activates the channel, making it nearly insensitive to the presence or absence of Ca2+.
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential measurements.

claim: The W287F mutation constitutively activates the channel, making it nearly insensitive to the presence or absence of Ca2+.
source: Whilst BEST1345 W287F retained normal Cl- versus K+ selectivity (Figure 4B), the W287F mutation constitutively activates the channel, making it nearly insensitive to the presence or absence of Ca2+.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing current maintained in the absence of Ca2+.

claim: Approximately 80% of the Cl- current level through BEST1345 W287F is maintained when Ca2+ was chelated with EGTA, whereas currents through wild type BEST1 drop to zero.
source: Approximately, 80% of the Cl- current level through BEST1345 W287F is maintained when Ca2+ was chelated with EGTA, whereas currents through wild type BEST1 drop to zero (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of BEST1345 W287F in the presence and absence of Ca2+ were determined at 2.7 Å and 3.0 Å resolutions, respectively.
source: To understand the molecular basis of this behavior, we determined cryo-EM structures of BEST1345 W287F in the presence and absence of Ca2+ at 2.7 Å and 3.0 Å resolutions, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: In the presence of Ca2+, BEST1345 W287F adopts an open conformation that is essentially indistinguishable from the open conformation observed for BEST1345.
source: In the presence of Ca2+, BEST1345 W287F adopts an open conformation that is essentially indistinguishable from the open conformation observed for BEST1345 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Cα RMSD = 0.2 Å).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison showing RMSD of 0.2 Å.

claim: 3D classification of the BEST1345 W287F dataset did not reveal a closed conformation, which indicates that essentially all of the particles are in an open conformation.
source: Unlike BEST1345, 3D classification of the BEST1345 W287F dataset did not reveal a closed conformation, which indicates that essentially all of the particles are in an open conformation and that the open state is preferential for this mutant.
evidence: This is supported by 3D classification analysis.

claim: The open state is preferential for the BEST1345 W287F mutant.
source: Unlike BEST1345, 3D classification of the BEST1345 W287F dataset did not reveal a closed conformation, which indicates that essentially all of the particles are in an open conformation and that the open state is preferential for this mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of closed conformations in 3D classification.

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, and in spite of missing density for Ca2+ and a disordered Ca2+-clasp region, the neck of BEST1345 W287F also adopts an open conformation.
source: Remarkably, in the absence of Ca2+, and in spite of missing density for Ca2+ and a disordered Ca2+-clasp region, the neck also adopts an open conformation (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The W287F mutation decouples Ca2+ binding from the conformational changes in the neck that are observed for the wild type channel.
source: Thus, in accord with the electrophysiological recordings, the W287F mutation decouples Ca2+ binding from the conformational changes in the neck that are observed for the wild type channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and electrophysiological data.

claim: Modeling of the W287F mutation on a closed conformation of the channel introduces a void behind the neck.
source: Modeling of the W287F mutation on a closed conformation of the channel introduces a void behind the neck (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E), which we hypothesize energetically disfavors the closed conformation.
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling.

claim: The void introduced by the W287F mutation energetically disfavors the closed conformation.
source: Modeling of the W287F mutation on a closed conformation of the channel introduces a void behind the neck (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E), which we hypothesize energetically disfavors the closed conformation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the modeling results.

claim: The open pore of BEST1 comprises a 90 Å-long water-filled vestibule and a short constriction at the cytosolic aperture.
source: The structures reveal that the open pore of BEST1 comprises a 90 Å-long water-filled vestibule and a short constriction at the cytosolic aperture (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is measured from the structures.

claim: The aperture is located approximately 55 Å from the neck.
source: The aperture, which is located approximately 55 Å from the neck, is only ~3 Å long (measured where the pore diameter is <4 Å); its walls are formed solely by the V205 side chains of the five subunits (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is measured from the structures.

claim: The aperture is only ~3 Å long (measured where the pore diameter is <4 Å).
source: The aperture, which is located approximately 55 Å from the neck, is only ~3 Å long (measured where the pore diameter is <4 Å); its walls are formed solely by the V205 side chains of the five subunits (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is measured from the structures.

claim: The walls of the aperture are formed solely by the V205 side chains of the five subunits.
source: The aperture, which is located approximately 55 Å from the neck, is only ~3 Å long (measured where the pore diameter is <4 Å); its walls are formed solely by the V205 side chains of the five subunits (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed from the structures.

claim: Retinitis pigmentosa can be caused by mutation of the corresponding I205 residue of human BEST1 to threonine.
source: Retinitis pigmentosa can be caused by mutation of the corresponding I205 residue of human BEST1 to threonine (Davidson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The aperture adopts the same conformation in all of the structures of BEST1 determined to date, regardless of whether the neck is open or closed or whether or not Ca2+ is bound.
source: The aperture adopts the same conformation in all of the structures of BEST1 determined to date, regardless of whether the neck is open or closed or whether or not Ca2+ is bound (Figure 1C,D, Figure 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The aperture does not function as either the activation or the inactivation gate.
source: We have concluded previously from electrophysiological studies that the aperture does not function as either the activation or the inactivation gate (Vaisey and Long, 2018; Vaisey et al., 2016), and the structural data support this conclusion.
evidence: This is supported by cited electrophysiological studies and structural data.

claim: The V205A mutation of chicken BEST1 has no effect on Ca2+-dependent activation or inactivation.
source: Accordingly, the V205A mutation of chicken BEST1, which would be expected to widen the aperture markedly, has no effect on Ca2+-dependent activation or inactivation (Vaisey and Long, 2018; Vaisey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Mutations of V205 have dramatic effects on ion permeability.
source: Mutations of V205 do, however, have dramatic effects on ion permeability (Vaisey et al., 2016) (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements.

claim: Both human and chicken BEST1 exhibit a lyotropic relative permeability sequence in which permeable anions that are more easily dehydrated than Cl-, such as Br-, I- and SCN-, are more permeable than Cl-.
source: Both human and chicken BEST1 exhibit a lyotropic relative permeability sequence in which permeable anions that are more easily dehydrated than Cl-, such as Br-, I- and SCN-, are more permeable than Cl- (Vaisey et al., 2016; Qu and Hartzell, 2000; Hartzell et al., 2005; Hille, 2001) (Figure 5C, PX/PCl ~ 2.7 when X = Br, ~5.1 when X = I and ~14.4 when X = SCN).
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements and cited references.

claim: The lyotropic permeability sequence is an indication that at least partial dehydration occurs for ions as they permeate through the channel.
source: The lyotropic permeability sequence is an indication that at least partial dehydration occurs for ions as they permeate through the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the permeability data and is established knowledge.

claim: The aperture is the only constriction where dehydration would occur in the open channel.
source: Given the structural context of the open channel, the aperture is the only constriction where dehydration would occur (Figure 1D,E); the dimensions of the aperture are too narrow for a hydrated ion to pass and therefore the aperture would necessitate that anions shed at least some water molecules as they pass through it.
evidence: This is inferred from the pore dimensions.

claim: The dimensions of the aperture are too narrow for a hydrated ion to pass.
source: Given the structural context of the open channel, the aperture is the only constriction where dehydration would occur (Figure 1D,E); the dimensions of the aperture are too narrow for a hydrated ion to pass and therefore the aperture would necessitate that anions shed at least some water molecules as they pass through it.
evidence: This is inferred from the measured dimensions of the aperture.

claim: The aperture necessitates that anions shed at least some water molecules as they pass through it.
source: Given the structural context of the open channel, the aperture is the only constriction where dehydration would occur (Figure 1D,E); the dimensions of the aperture are too narrow for a hydrated ion to pass and therefore the aperture would necessitate that anions shed at least some water molecules as they pass through it.
evidence: This is inferred from the dimensions of the aperture.

claim: The aperture is responsible for the lyotropic permeability sequence.
source: The structures support the conclusion that the aperture is responsible for the lyotropic permeability sequence (Vaisey et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and the cited reference.

claim: Mutation of V205 to a smaller residue (e.g. glycine, alanine, or serine) abolishes the lyotropic sequence among Cl-, Br-, I- and SCN-.
source: Consistently, we find that mutation of V205 to a smaller residue (e.g. glycine, alanine, or serine) abolishes the lyotropic sequence among Cl-, Br-, I- and SCN- (Figure 5C), which suggests that the aperture is made sufficiently wide by these mutations to allow these ions to pass without dehydration.
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements.

claim: The aperture is made sufficiently wide by mutations to glycine, alanine, or serine to allow Cl-, Br-, I- and SCN- to pass without dehydration.
source: Consistently, we find that mutation of V205 to a smaller residue (e.g. glycine, alanine, or serine) abolishes the lyotropic sequence among Cl-, Br-, I- and SCN- (Figure 5C), which suggests that the aperture is made sufficiently wide by these mutations to allow these ions to pass without dehydration.
evidence: This is inferred from the permeability data.

claim: Mutation of V205 to isoleucine makes the lyotropic permeability differences between Cl-, Br-, I- and SCN- more dramatic.
source: In contrast to the effects of small amino acids, mutation of V205 to isoleucine, a bulkier hydrophobic amino acid that would presumably reduce the diameter of the aperture, makes the lyotropic permeability differences between Cl-, Br-, I- and SCN- more dramatic (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements.

claim: Ions shed more water molecules when passing through the V205I aperture than through the wild type one.
source: These effects suggest that ions would shed more water molecules when passing through the V205I aperture than through the wild type one.
evidence: This is inferred from the permeability data.

claim: The aperture controls permeability among halide anions by causing ion dehydration.
source: Thus, the aperture controls permeability among halide anions by causing ion dehydration, and it thereby engenders the characteristic lyotropic permeability sequence of BEST1.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and permeability data.

claim: The aperture engenders the characteristic lyotropic permeability sequence of BEST1.
source: Thus, the aperture controls permeability among halide anions by causing ion dehydration, and it thereby engenders the characteristic lyotropic permeability sequence of BEST1.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and permeability data.

claim: The relative permeability of the channel to acetate, propionate and butyrate increases when V205 is substituted with the smaller alanine or glycine residues.
source: We found that the relative permeability of the channel to acetate, propionate and butyrate increases when V205 is substituted with the smaller alanine or glycine residues (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements.

claim: When the aperture is made wider by mutation, larger organic anions are more permeable.
source: Thus, when the aperture is made wider by mutation, larger organic anions are more permeable.
evidence: This is inferred from the permeability data.

claim: The aperture functions in the wild type channel as a size-selective filter.
source: These data support the previous inference (Vaisey et al., 2016) that the aperture functions in the wild type channel as a size-selective filter.
evidence: This is supported by permeability data and the cited reference.

claim: The aperture would tend to prevent the permeation of large cellular constituents such as proteins or nucleic acids but would allow smaller solutes such as Cl- ions to pass.
source: The aperture would tend to prevent the permeation of large cellular constituents such as proteins or nucleic acids but would allow smaller solutes such as Cl- ions to pass.
evidence: This is inferred from the size-selective properties of the aperture.

claim: The aperture is not perfectly discriminatory for the smallest solutes, as indicated by the measureable permeability of the wild type channel to acetate.
source: However, the data indicate that the aperture is not perfectly discriminatory for the smallest solutes, as indicated by the measureable permeability of the wild type channel to acetate (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements.

claim: The amino acid sequence at and around amino acid 205 varies among human BEST1-4 channels and among bestrophin channels in general.
source: Notably, the amino acid sequence at and around amino acid 205 varies among human BEST1-4 channels and among bestrophin channels in general (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment.

claim: Sequence variability at the aperture may endow BEST1-4 channels with distinct permeabilities related to their specific physiological functions and their particular biological locations.
source: This sequence variability at the aperture may endow BEST1-4 channels with distinct permeabilities related to their specific physiological functions and their particular biological locations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the sequence variability and permeability data.

claim: The structures represent the major gating transitions in the metazoan bestrophin channel.
source: The structures presented herein represent the major gating transitions in the metazoan bestrophin channel.
evidence: This is supported by the multiple conformational states captured.

claim: When unoccupied by Ca2+, the Ca2+ clasps are disordered, the neck is closed, and ions are prevented from permeating through the channel by the neck.
source: When unoccupied by Ca2+, the Ca2+ clasps are disordered, the neck is closed, and ions are prevented from permeating through the channel by the neck.
evidence: This is supported by the Ca2+-free structure.

claim: When Ca2+ ions bind, the Ca2+ clasps become ordered and the open and closed conformations of the channel have free energies that are similar enough that the neck can sample both conformations.
source: When Ca2+ ions bind, the Ca2+ clasps become ordered and the open and closed conformations of the channel have free energies that are similar enough that the neck can sample both conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of both open and closed conformations in the Ca2+-bound dataset.

claim: The open conformation of the neck is dramatically wider than the closed conformation.
source: The open conformation of the neck is dramatically wider than the closed conformation and opening (activation) exposes small hydrophilic amino acids to the pore where large hydrophobic ones had been.
evidence: This is supported by pore dimension analysis.

claim: Opening (activation) exposes small hydrophilic amino acids to the pore where large hydrophobic ones had been.
source: The open conformation of the neck is dramatically wider than the closed conformation and opening (activation) exposes small hydrophilic amino acids to the pore where large hydrophobic ones had been.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: The wide neck explains why the neck has essentially no influence on ion selectivity.
source: The wide neck explains why the neck has essentially no influence on ion selectivity (Vaisey et al., 2016), in spite of speculation that it might be involved in ion selectivity from the initial X-ray structure of BEST1 (Kane Dickson et al., 2014) and the structure of KpBest (Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the wide dimensions of the open neck and cited references.

claim: The channel inactivates at higher concentrations of Ca2+ through a mechanism that involves the binding of the C-terminal inactivation peptide to its receptor.
source: The channel inactivates at higher concentrations of Ca2+ through a mechanism that involves the binding of the C-terminal inactivation peptide to its receptor.
evidence: This is supported by structural data and cited references.

claim: The receptor for the inactivation peptide is on the cytosolic surface of the channel.
source: The receptor is on the cytosolic surface of the channel and the binding of the inactivation peptide to it allosterically controls the conformation of the neck from a distance.
evidence: This is observed from the structures.

claim: The binding of the inactivation peptide to its receptor allosterically controls the conformation of the neck from a distance.
source: The receptor is on the cytosolic surface of the channel and the binding of the inactivation peptide to it allosterically controls the conformation of the neck from a distance.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing the inactivation peptide bound and the neck closed.

claim: The inactivated conformation of the neck is indistinguishable from the deactivated (Ca2+-free) one.
source: The inactivated conformation of the neck is indistinguishable from the deactivated (Ca2+-free) one.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: Unlike voltage-dependent K+ and Na+ channels, in which ions are prevented from flowing by different mechanisms in the inactivated and deactivated states, the same closed conformation of the neck is responsible for the deactivated and inactivated states of BEST1.
source: Unlike voltage-dependent K+ and Na+ channels, in which ions are prevented from flowing by different mechanisms in the inactivated and deactivated states (Hille, 2001; Armstrong and Bezanilla, 1977), the same closed conformation of the neck is responsible for the deactivated and inactivated states of BEST1.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and cited references.

claim: BEST1 does not contain separable domains.
source: Unlike many ion channels that have separate self-contained domains that are responsible for controlling channel gating, such as extracellular or intracellular ligand-binding domains, or voltage sensor domains within the membrane, which can often be studied in isolation using structural or functional approaches, BEST1 does not contain separable domains.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural architecture.

claim: The BEST1 channel comprises a single structural unit that resembles a barrel, with a portion of the barrel embedded in the membrane and a portion exposed to the cytosol.
source: The BEST1 channel comprises a single structural unit that resembles a barrel, with a portion of the barrel embedded in the membrane and a portion exposed to the cytosol.
evidence: This is observed from the structures.

claim: The primary sequence of BEST1 does not have separate domains; rather the polypeptide portions that form the transmembrane and cytosolic regions of the channel are dispersed throughout the primary sequence.
source: Additionally, the primary sequence of BEST1 does not have separate domains; rather the polypeptide portions that form the transmembrane and cytosolic regions of the channel are dispersed throughout the primary sequence (Kane Dickson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and the cited reference.

claim: The midsection of the barrel contains the region that functions as a gate (the neck).
source: The midsection of the barrel contains the region that functions as a gate (the neck) and the cytosolic surface of the barrel is decorated with sensors that influence the gate – namely the Ca2+ clasps and the inactivation peptide receptors.
evidence: This is observed from the structures.

claim: The cytosolic surface of the barrel is decorated with sensors that influence the gate – namely the Ca2+ clasps and the inactivation peptide receptors.
source: The midsection of the barrel contains the region that functions as a gate (the neck) and the cytosolic surface of the barrel is decorated with sensors that influence the gate – namely the Ca2+ clasps and the inactivation peptide receptors.
evidence: This is observed from the structures.

claim: The sensors function as integral parts of the channel as a whole and could not be studied in isolation.
source: These sensors, which function as integral parts of the channel as a whole and could not be studied in isolation, modulate the energetics of opening and closing of the neck through allosteric means.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural architecture.

claim: The sensors modulate the energetics of opening and closing of the neck through allosteric means.
source: These sensors, which function as integral parts of the channel as a whole and could not be studied in isolation, modulate the energetics of opening and closing of the neck through allosteric means.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and functional studies.

claim: The sensors relay information received at the surface of the channel, such as the binding of Ca2+ or the inactivation peptide, through the core of the protein to the neck.
source: The sensors do so by relaying information received at the surface of the channel, such as the binding of Ca2+ or the inactivation peptide, through the core of the protein to the neck.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: The design of the neck appears well suited to receive subtle energetic information in that the neck comprises five helices (the S2b neck helices) that are tethered on each end by linker regions that allow the helices to toggle between two preferred orientations that form the closed and open conformations of the neck.
source: The design of the neck itself appears well suited to receive this subtle energetic information in that the neck comprises five helices (the S2b neck helices) that are tethered on each end by linker regions that allow the helices to toggle between two preferred orientations that form the closed and open conformations of the neck.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural features of the neck.

claim: In bestrophin, cytosolic sensors on the surface of the channel control a dramatic molecular choreography within the core of the protein that underlies gating and reveals a fascinating new gating mechanism among ion channels.
source: Thus, while localized twisting or domain motions that are instigated by separate sensor domains often constitute the activation mechanism of ion channels, in bestrophin cytosolic sensors on the surface of the channel control a dramatic molecular choreography within the core of the protein that underlies gating and reveals a fascinating new gating mechanism among ion channels.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the structural data presented.

claim: The electrophysiological and structural data suggest that the aperture remains essentially fixed throughout the Ca2+-dependent activation and inactivation processes.
source: Our electrophysiological and structural data suggest that the aperture remains essentially fixed throughout the Ca2+-dependent activation and inactivation processes.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and functional data.

claim: The aperture functions as a size-selective filter that discriminates permeant species on the basis of size and dehydration energy.
source: Rather than functioning as a gate, as has been proposed (Yang et al., 2014), our data indicate that the aperture functions as a size-selective filter that discriminates permeant species on the basis of size and dehydration energy.
evidence: This is supported by permeability data and structural analysis.

claim: The dimensions and hydrophobicity of the aperture are such that any ion or hydrophilic entity passing through it must be at least partially dehydrated to fit.
source: Its dimensions and its hydrophobicity are such that any ion or hydrophilic entity passing through it must be at least partially dehydrated to fit.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural dimensions and properties of the aperture.

claim: The aperture is responsible for the lyotropic permeability sequence among small anions (e.g. Cl-, Br-, I-, SCN-) in which ions that are more easily dehydrated are more permeable through the channel.
source: The aperture is thereby responsible for the lyotropic permeability sequence among small anions (e.g. Cl-, Br-, I-, SCN-) in which ions that are more easily dehydrated are more permeable through the channel.
evidence: This is supported by permeability data and structural analysis.

claim: The aperture limits the flow of larger anions such as acetate and mutations that increase the width of the aperture allow such ions to permeate more readily.
source: The aperture also limits the flow of larger anions such as acetate and mutations that increase the width of the aperture allow such ions to permeate more readily.
evidence: This is supported by permeability data.

claim: It has been proposed that the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA permeates through BEST1 and underlies a tonic form of synaptic inhibition in glia.
source: It has been proposed that the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA permeates through BEST1 and underlies a tonic form of synaptic inhibition in glia (Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The widened neck of the open channel conformation makes the possibility of slow conductance of GABA and/or other larger solutes more plausible from a structural perspective.
source: Previously, this possibility seemed incongruous with the narrowness of the neck observed in the X-ray structure (Kane Dickson et al., 2014) but the widened neck of the open channel conformation makes the possibility of slow conductance of GABA and/or other larger solutes more plausible from a structural perspective.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data.

claim: Thermal motions that transiently widen the aperture may allow slow permeation of molecules the size of GABA at physiologically relevant rates.
source: While the dimensions of the aperture in the atomic models of BEST1, based on the cryo-EM and X-ray studies, would appear to preclude permeation of molecules the size of GABA, thermal motions that transiently widen the aperture may allow slow permeation of such solutes at physiologically relevant rates.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural data.

claim: It is conceivable that regulatory mechanisms that influence the aperture exist and would modulate permeation of larger solutes.
source: Further, it is conceivable that regulatory mechanisms that influence the aperture exist and would modulate such permeation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The sequence diversity in the aperture region may give rise to distinct permeation properties among bestrophins.
source: Given the importance of the aperature in regulating permeation, the sequence diversity in the aperture region is particularly intriguing. This diversity may give rise to distinct permeation properties among bestrophins and hints that the physiological functions of the channels are broader and more nuanced than currently appreciated.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on sequence analysis and permeability data.

claim: The sequence diversity in the aperture region hints that the physiological functions of the channels are broader and more nuanced than currently appreciated.
source: Given the importance of the aperature in regulating permeation, the sequence diversity in the aperture region is particularly intriguing. This diversity may give rise to distinct permeation properties among bestrophins and hints that the physiological functions of the channels are broader and more nuanced than currently appreciated.
evidence: This is speculation based on sequence diversity and functional considerations.
